description: We’re building a tool that combines NASA Earth observations with local agricultural data to help farmers explore crop rotations, protect soil, and adapt to changing conditions. We’re looking for teammates interested in agriculture, GIS, remote sensing, data analysis, web development, UI/UX, and storytelling. Join us to learn, share ideas, and turn satellite data into practical insights for farmers. Curiosity, commitment, and teamwork are welcome!
summary:
Agroshift is a web app that turns open NASA Earth observation data into simple crop-rotation advice for small and medium rice farmers in Daule, Ecuador, the heart of the country's rice production. Farmers there plant rice after rice, two or three times a year, while rainfall no longer follows the old calendar: in October 2026, in the middle of the dry season, NASA GPM IMERG recorded 585 mm of rain.

We combined NASA POWER (daily climate), GPM IMERG (rainfall), Landsat 8 and 9 (monthly vegetation, surface water and moisture indices over five years) and SRTM (elevation). Using Google Earth Engine and Python, we clipped the imagery to the study area, grouped the land into three zones with K-means (flood-prone lowland, slope and dry hill), classified each rainy season as very wet, normal or dry, and estimated irrigation needs with the FAO-56 method.

The app compares three strategies (rice-rice, rice-soybean and a two-year rice/maize-soybean rotation) for each zone and type of year, and explains its recommendation with evidence, benefits, information gaps and risks, in plain language and mobile-friendly. It supports, not replaces, farmer and local agronomist judgment, and can scale to any region with open NASA data.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Agroshift is a mobile-first web app that helps small and medium rice farmers in Daule, Ecuador, decide what to plant, when and where. Daule is the heart of Ecuador's rice production, and most farmers plant rice after rice, two or three times a year. Rainfall no longer follows the old calendar: in October 2026, in the middle of the dry season, NASA GPM IMERG recorded 585 mm of rain. Agroshift turns open NASA data into plain-language advice that a farmer can read on a phone.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Data: NASA POWER (daily rainfall, temperature and radiation), GPM IMERG (monthly rainfall), Landsat 8 and 9 (monthly NDVI, NDWI and NDMI composites from November 2021 to October 2026) and SRTM (elevation and slope).

2. Processing: Google Earth Engine clips the imagery to the study area, masks clouds with QA_PIXEL and builds monthly median composites, so we never download full 1 GB scenes. Months without a clean image (such as January 2024) are shown as gaps, not filled with invented values.

3. Analysis (Python): K-means clustering groups the land into three zones (flood-prone lowland, slope and dry hill). Each rainy season is classified as very wet, normal or dry using IMERG. Crop water needs are estimated with the FAO-56 method (Kc × ET0 minus effective rainfall), using crop cycles and coefficients from a local crop catalog.

4. Decision support: the app compares three strategies (rice-rice, rice-soybean, and a two-year rice/maize-soybean rotation) for each zone and type of year. It ranks them according to what the farmer cares about most (saving water, soil health, fewer pests, income) and explains the recommendation with evidence, benefits, information gaps and risks, plus simple field rules backed by data.

5. Interface: "My farm" shows what to do this month and a 12-month crop calendar; "My field" shows the satellite view over time; "Options" compares the strategies; "Recommendation" explains the choice; and an illustrated dashboard summarizes all the data.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- Helps farmers plan rotations that use less irrigation water, add nitrogen to the soil and break pest cycles.

- Warns about flooding risk in low areas and about very wet or dry years.

- Uses only free, open NASA data, so it can scale to any region by changing the study area. The same engine could support the Ecuadorian Andes (potato, lupin and broad bean rotations), with slope as the main factor.

- Can be used by farmer associations, agricultural technicians and public agencies.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

Python (pandas, NumPy, xarray, rasterio, scikit-learn, shapely), Google Earth Engine Python API, NASA POWER API, QGIS, Streamlit, Plotly, Folium/Leaflet, Docker, Git and GitHub. The app is packaged in a Docker container so it can run on any server or laptop. No special hardware was required.

CREATIVITY

Instead of showing raw indices, Agroshift translates satellite data into a farmer's language: a visual year calendar with crop icons, traffic-light signals, priorities chosen with buttons, and a map that works like a simple GIS (layers for zones, elevation and slope). Every number shows where it comes from.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Data resolution: POWER, IMERG and SMAP describe the area, not a single plot; inside the plot we only use 30 m data.

- Clouds: the rainy season leaves gaps in Landsat imagery, and the app shows them honestly.

- Local reality: many farmers keep rice because it has a secure market and their soils flood; the app shows these risks instead of hiding them.

- Validation: crop values and rules must be confirmed with local agronomists (INIAP) and farmers. Agroshift supports, but does not replace, their judgment.

- Accessibility: plain Spanish, a highly legible font, large buttons and a mobile-first design.

TEAM

Mario, Thomas, Austin, Johan and Andrés.
